newsitem.title: CHINA: China takes six into custody over banned novel.
newsitem.headline: China takes six into custody over banned novel.

text.p: Chinese police have detained six people over a banned novel with a plot strikingly similar to a corruption scandal that led to the downfall of the most senior official under communist rule, Chinese sources said on Sunday.

Beijing police took the six, including a man surnamed Hu and his girlfriend, in for questioning last month for their involvement in the publishing, printing and circulation of the novel "Wrath of Heaven", said the sources who asked not to be identified.

China's propaganda tsars have banned "Wrath of Heaven", which recounts the tale of a graft-buster who runs into huge difficulties while investigating a corruption scandal after the mysterious death of a vice-mayor.

The "Wrath of Heaven" has become a bestseller because its plot bears a striking resemblance to the disgrace of Chen Xitong, who resigned as Beijing's Communist Party boss in April 1995 after his protege, vice-mayor Wang Baosen, committed suicide after coming under investigation for corruption.
It was unclear if the authorities planned to prosecute the author, Chen Fang, who is not related to the disgraced Beijing Communist Party boss. He wrote the novel under the pseudonym Fang Wen.

Chen Fang, 53, is a Beijing-based author whose works include "Woman", a novel about the murder of a model. He was former editor-in-chief of the now-defunct Chinese-language magazine "The World of Chinese" and writes television and film scripts.
Chinese authorities raided a printing plant in Tongxian county in suburban Beijing in April and seized plates used to print the novel, the sources said.
The authorities have sought to dismiss the president and editor-in-chief of the publisher, Wan Fang Publishing House in the northern region of Inner Mongolia, the sources said.
But Ge Fu, president of the publishing house, has refused to step down, demanding that the authorities first determine whether the novel was "reactionary", they said.
Chinese officials, the publishing house and the author could not be reached for comment.
Tens of thousands of pirated copies of the banned novel have found their way on to the shelves of small bookshops in Beijing. The novel is also a hit in many other parts of China.

Chen Xitong, 67, is the most senior official to be ensnared in a corruption scandal since the communists swept to power in 1949. He was ousted from the Communist Party's powerful Politburo in September 1995 and has not been seen in public since April 1995.
Hong Kong's China-watching newspapers say he is under house arrest in Inner Mongolia after losing out in a power struggle with China's Communist Party chief Jiang Zemin.
One of Chen Xitong's sons has been detained for corruption and his mistress remains on the run.
Corruption, virtually unknown in China under the rule of the late party chairman Mao Zedong, has made a rapid comeback in nearly two decades of market reform.
In January, China's propaganda tsars moved to eradicate ideas out of line with Communist Party ideology, ordering publishers to issue more good books.
